designs.label: Midtown
designs.name: Midtown Manhattan
designs.story: The Atelier's second study of the real skyline: Midtown, where the island's grid fills with the tallest buildings of their day. The Empire State Building rises off Fifth Avenue in grey setbacks to a mast at the ceiling; the Chrysler Building answers from the east with a silver crown; between them Grand Central's hall faces 42nd Street with the MetLife slab behind it and One Vanderbilt beside it. North along Fifth the Public Library's white columns look over Bryant Park, St Patrick's spire and the tan slab of 30 Rockefeller Plaza stand off Sixth Avenue, and the Plaza and Carnegie Hall close the north. Times Square's bright towers flank a small square, the Waldorf and the Seagram Building keep the east, the Flatiron's narrow prow and Madison Square Garden the south.

designs.label: Central Park
designs.name: Central Park
designs.story: The Atelier's second study of the real city: the park the island keeps at its heart, drawn round the glass's own lake. A meadow where the sheep once grazed, a tree-lined mall to a terrace over the water, a castle on the rocks that reads the weather, a lawn the size of a village, an obelisk older than the city, a museum on the avenue, and the small animals of bronze that children climb.

designs.label: Uptown
designs.name: Uptown Manhattan
designs.story: The Atelier's third study of the real city: Uptown, north of the park. On the heights by the Hudson the Cloisters keep their medieval walls, Grant's Tomb looks over the river and Riverside Church raises the tallest church tower in the country; Columbia's domed library and the unfinished cathedral of St John the Divine stand east of Broadway. Harlem fills the middle: the three brick rows of Strivers' Row, the Apollo's marquee on 125th Street, Morningside Park under its cliff and the Harlem Meer at the park's corner. The East Side keeps the trains on their viaduct over Park Avenue, the Guggenheim's white spiral and the mayor's wooden house above the river.

sections.name: The Plaza Hotel
sections.signText: The Plaza Hotel: a French chateau of 1907 at the corner of the park; its tea court and its guests have filled novels and films.

sections.name: Carnegie Hall
sections.signText: Carnegie Hall: built in 1891 with a steel baron's money and opened by Tchaikovsky; the joke about reaching it is older than most of its musicians.

sections.name: St Patrick's Cathedral
sections.signText: St Patrick's Cathedral: white marble in the Gothic manner, begun in 1858 on what was then the edge of town, its spires finished in 1888.

sections.name: 30 Rockefeller Plaza
sections.signText: 30 Rockefeller Plaza: the tall slab of a city within the city, raised through the Depression in 1933; a skating rink sits at its feet.

sections.name: One Vanderbilt
sections.signText: One Vanderbilt: a glass tower of 2020 beside the terminal, its point among the highest in Midtown.

sections.name: The MetLife Building
sections.signText: The MetLife Building: the wide slab of 1963 standing astride Park Avenue behind the terminal, once the largest office building in the world.

sections.name: Grand Central Terminal
sections.signText: Grand Central Terminal: a railway hall of 1913 under a painted sky of stars; forty-four platforms lie beneath the streets around it.

sections.name: The Chrysler Building
sections.signText: The Chrysler Building: steel eagles and a crown of silver arches, finished in 1930; the spire was assembled inside and raised in secret to win the race for height.

sections.name: One Times Square
sections.signText: One Times Square: a slim tower of 1904 built for a newspaper; since 1907 a lit ball has dropped down its pole at midnight on the last day of the year.

sections.name: Duffy Square
sections.signText: Duffy Square: the small triangle at the head of Times Square, named for a wartime chaplain; its steps look down the lights.

sections.name: The Paramount Building
sections.signText: The Paramount Building: a film company's tower of 1927 with a clock and a glass globe at the top, setbacks all the way up.

sections.name: Bryant Park
sections.signText: Bryant Park: a lawn behind the library on the site of a reservoir; the books are kept in stacks beneath the grass.

sections.name: The New York Public Library
sections.signText: The New York Public Library: white marble opened in 1911, two stone lions at the steps named Patience and Fortitude.

sections.name: The Waldorf Astoria
sections.signText: The Waldorf Astoria: the hotel of 1931 on Park Avenue, twin towers over a block; presidents kept suites here.

sections.name: The Seagram Building
sections.signText: The Seagram Building: bronze and dark glass of 1958, set back from the avenue behind a plaza that became the rule.

sections.name: The Flatiron Building
sections.signText: The Flatiron Building: a narrow triangle of 1902 where Broadway crosses Fifth, twenty-two storeys on a prow six feet wide.

sections.name: The Empire State Building
sections.signText: The Empire State Building: 102 storeys of limestone raised in 410 days and finished in 1931; the mast was meant for airships and holds the lights instead.

sections.name: Madison Square Garden
sections.signText: Madison Square Garden: the round arena of 1968 over the railway station, the fourth to carry the name.

sections.name: Sheep Meadow
sections.signText: Sheep Meadow: fifteen acres of lawn where a flock grazed until 1934, kept by a shepherd who lived at the Dairy; now the park's great picnic ground.

sections.name: The Dairy
sections.signText: The Dairy: a Gothic cottage of 1870 that sold fresh milk to the city's children; today the park's visitor centre.

sections.name: The Carousel
sections.signText: The Carousel: fifty-seven hand-carved horses of 1908, found in a Coney Island trolley barn and turning here since 1951.

sections.name: Wollman Rink
sections.signText: Wollman Rink: an open sheet of ice since 1950 with the skyline for a backdrop; a pool and a playground when the ice goes.

sections.name: The Central Park Zoo
sections.signText: The Central Park Zoo: a menagerie since the 1860s, rebuilt in 1988 round a sea lion pool; penguins, snow monkeys and a red panda live here.

sections.name: Bethesda Terrace
sections.signText: Bethesda Terrace: the park's one formal set piece, sandstone stairs and an arcade of 1864 facing the water, carved with the birds and seasons.

sections.name: The Angel of the Waters, Bethesda Fountain
sections.signText: The Angel of the Waters: the fountain's bronze figure of 1873, the first public sculpture in the city by a woman, Emma Stebbins.

sections.name: Alice in Wonderland
sections.signText: Alice in Wonderland: a bronze of 1959 at the Conservatory Water, cast with the Mad Hatter and the March Hare, polished bright by climbing children.

sections.name: Belvedere Castle
sections.signText: Belvedere Castle: a folly of 1869 on the park's highest rock, a lookout by design; the city's weather has been measured from its tower since 1919.

sections.name: The Loeb Boathouse
sections.signText: The Loeb Boathouse: rowing boats for hire on the lake since 1954, from a boathouse given by a banker who loved the water.

sections.name: Strawberry Fields
sections.signText: Strawberry Fields: a quiet garden on the park's west side, laid out in 1985 in memory of a musician who lived across the street.

sections.name: The Imagine mosaic
sections.signText: The Imagine mosaic: a circle of black and white stone laid by craftsmen from Naples in 1985, with one word at its centre.

sections.name: Balto
sections.signText: Balto: the bronze sled dog of 1925, raised the year his team carried serum across Alaska to Nome through a blizzard.

sections.name: The Great Lawn
sections.signText: The Great Lawn: fifty-five acres of grass over the bed of the old receiving reservoir, drained in 1931; ball fields by day, concerts by night.

sections.name: The Obelisk, Cleopatra's Needle
sections.signText: The Obelisk: a granite needle of 1450 BC, raised at Heliopolis, moved to Alexandria by Rome, and set here in 1881, the oldest made thing in the city.

sections.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art
sections.signText: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: founded in 1870 and on the park's edge since 1880; its Fifth Avenue front of 1902 hides a red-brick hall behind.

sections.name: The Cloisters
sections.signText: The Cloisters: the Metropolitan Museum's house of medieval art, opened in 1938 on a hill above the Hudson and built round cloisters carried stone by stone from French abbeys.

sections.name: Grant's Tomb
sections.signText: Grant's Tomb: the resting place of Ulysses S. Grant, general and president, and his wife Julia; finished in 1897 with gifts from some ninety thousand people.

sections.name: Riverside Church
sections.signText: Riverside Church: a Gothic church of 1930 paid for by John D. Rockefeller Jr.; its tower, the tallest of any church in the country, holds a carillon of seventy-four bells.

sections.name: The American Museum of Natural History
sections.signText: The American Museum of Natural History: founded in 1869 on the park's west side; dinosaur skeletons fill its upper halls and a life-size blue whale hangs over the ocean hall.

sections.name: The Rose Center for Earth and Space
sections.signText: The Rose Center for Earth and Space: the museum's glass cube of 2000, with a white sphere hung inside it that holds the planetarium's dome.

sections.name: Low Memorial Library, Columbia University
sections.signText: Low Memorial Library: Columbia's domed hall of 1897, given by its president Seth Low in memory of his father; the books left for a new library in 1934 and the offices moved in.

sections.name: The Cathedral of St John the Divine
sections.signText: The Cathedral of St John the Divine: begun in 1892 and never finished; its builders changed from the Romanesque to the Gothic halfway up, and it is among the largest churches anywhere.

sections.name: Morningside Park
sections.signText: Morningside Park: drawn by Olmsted and Vaux, the makers of Central Park, along the cliff that parts Morningside Heights from Harlem; long stone stairs climb the rock.

sections.name: Strivers' Row: the red brick houses
sections.signText: Strivers' Row: James Brown Lord's red brick houses, one of three rows that a developer, David King, had three architects build together on 138th and 139th Streets in 1891.

sections.name: Strivers' Row: the yellow brick houses
sections.signText: Strivers' Row: Bruce Price and Clarence Luce's yellow brick houses with white stone trim; the alleys behind them still bear old notices asking riders to lead their horses.

sections.name: Strivers' Row: the dark brick houses
sections.signText: Strivers' Row: Stanford White's dark brick houses; in the 1920s Black doctors, lawyers and musicians bought along these streets, and Harlem named the row for their ambition.

sections.name: The Apollo Theater
sections.signText: The Apollo Theater: a burlesque house of 1914 that opened to Black audiences in 1934; its Wednesday amateur nights launched Ella Fitzgerald and a long line of singers after her.

sections.name: The Harlem-125th Street station
sections.signText: The Harlem-125th Street station: since 1897 the trains to the northern suburbs have run above Park Avenue on a viaduct here, stopping once more before they cross the Harlem River.

sections.name: The Harlem Meer
sections.signText: The Harlem Meer: the pond at the park's north-east corner, its name Dutch for a lake, after the village of Harlem that the Dutch founded here in 1658.

sections.name: The Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum
sections.signText: The Guggenheim Museum: Frank Lloyd Wright's white spiral of 1959, one long ramp climbing past the paintings to a glass dome; Wright died six months before it opened.

sections.name: Gracie Mansion
sections.signText: Gracie Mansion: a merchant's wooden country house of 1799 above a swift channel of the East River, the official home of the city's mayors since 1942.

segments.note: Midtown's southern half for the Atelier's larger replica, from 34th Street up; the Empire State Building, Madison Square Garden and Penn Station, the Flatiron's head.
Midtown's northern half; 42nd Street with the Chrysler Building, Grand Central and the Public Library, Rockefeller Center, St Patrick's, Times Square.
Central Park's southern end for the Atelier; Sheep Meadow, the Mall, Bethesda Terrace by the lake, the Dairy and the carousel.
Central Park's northern half; Belvedere Castle over the lake, the Great Lawn, the Reservoir's shore, the Obelisk and the museum on Fifth Avenue.

Uptown's West Side, north of the park; the Cloisters, Grant's Tomb, Riverside Church and the Natural History Museum by the sea, Columbia's library and St John the Divine east of Broadway, Morningside Park.
Uptown's Harlem and East Side; Strivers' Row, the Apollo on 125th Street, the Harlem Meer, the station under the Park Avenue viaduct, the Guggenheim and Gracie Mansion.
